# Projections: which tool

Mera has more than one way to turn a simulation into a picture, and the names do not say which is
which. This page is a router: find the sentence that matches what you want, and follow it.

Everything here works the same on hydro and, unless noted, on particles.

## A single map

| I want | Use |
|---|---|
| a map along a box axis | `projection(gas, :sd; direction=:z)`, see [Hydro](06_hydro_Projection.md) / [Particles](06_particles_Projection.md) |
| a galaxy face-on or edge-on | `projection(gas, :sd; direction=:faceon)`, which derives the orientation from the data's own angular momentum. Restrict that sum with `angmom_radius`, or a whole-box `L` can tilt a "face-on" disc by tens of degrees |
| any other viewing angle | `inclination`/`azimuth` about a reference `axis`, or an explicit `los=[x,y,z]`, see [Off-axis](06_offaxis_Projection.md) |
| the disc's axis as a bare 3-vector | [`angmom`](@ref)`(gas; center=[:bc], radius=[10,:kpc])`, and `angmom([gas, stars, dm])` to set it from several components at once |
| the disc's axis as a ready-made frame | [`face_on`](@ref) / [`edge_on`](@ref), which return a frame whose `los`/`up`/`center` splat into any later call |
| the same window at every angle | `fov`/`fov_unit` with `aperture=:circle|:square`. Without it an off-axis projection fits its window to the rotated data, so the object appears to zoom between angles |

## Selecting a region first

`subregion` and `shellregion` work on **all six** data types, including RT and sinks, which have no
tutorial page of their own. One trap, documented in the
[Subregions API](api/subregions.md): neither function wraps at a periodic boundary, so a region
near a box face is silently clipped rather than wrapped.

## A cutting plane

A plane, not a column: values *at* a depth rather than integrated through it.

| I want | Use |
|---|---|
| a plane along a box axis | `slice(gas, :rho; slice_axis=:z, slice_pos=0.5)`, see [Covering grid](covering_grid.md) |
| a tilted plane | `slice(gas, :rho; inclination=…)`, the same view keywords as `projection` |
| the plane to travel through the object | `offset`/`offset_unit`, which slides it along the line of sight |
| the same for particles | you want `thickness`, not a plane, see below |

**Particles have no cutting plane, and that is not an omission.** A particle is a point, so a
zero-thickness plane through a particle cloud is empty by construction. The useful analogue is a
projection of finite depth: `projection(part, :sd; thickness=2, thickness_unit=:kpc)` integrates a
slab instead of the whole column, and `offset` moves the slab. Asking for zero thickness is
refused rather than returning an empty map.

## A movie

Three different movies, and the difference is what changes between frames.

| Between frames, what changes? | Use |
|---|---|
| **time**, one frame per snapshot | [`getmovie`](@ref)`(path, :sd)` |
| **angle**, one snapshot seen from many sides | [`rotation_sequence`](@ref), which fixes the frame so the object cannot drift |
| **both**: a full turn at each snapshot | `getmovie(…; angles=0:5:355)`, giving `outputs × angles` frames |
| **both**: turning while the run evolves | `getmovie(…; sweep=(0, 180))`, one frame per snapshot at a moving angle |

No frame is ever interpolated: each is a real projection from a real viewpoint.

Two things worth knowing before a long render. Pass `fov` for any off-axis movie, or the frame
refits per snapshot and the movie breathes. And `angles` keeps a snapshot in memory while its
viewpoints render, which is the one place `getmovie` gives up its one-snapshot-at-a-time frugality;
`sweep` does not.

Particle movies work: `getmovie(path, :sd; datatype=:particles)`. Gravity and clumps cannot be
projected on their own, and say so.

## Why there are two engines

`direction=:x/:y/:z` and the off-axis path are separate implementations, and the reason is
geometric rather than historical.

Seen down a box axis, a cell's shadow on the image plane is an axis-aligned **rectangle**, and the
overlap with a pixel is a product of two independent 1-D overlaps. That is what the axis-aligned
engine exploits: it bins in integer grid-index space, per refinement level, which is both exact and
fast.

Rotate the camera and the same cube casts a **hexagon**, because you now see three of its faces.
The overlap stops being separable and becomes an integral over a piecewise-linear height field, and
that is a different algorithm, the one `binning=:overlap`/`:exact` implement. It degenerates
correctly to the axis-aligned case when the line of sight is parallel to a box axis.

The hexagon is also what the choice of `binning` turns on, so
[the off-axis page](06_offaxis_Projection.md) works through it in more detail and measures what
each setting costs.

The practical consequences:

* the axis-aligned path does less work per cell, two 1-D clips rather than a polygon integral, so
  it should be the cheaper of the two. No measurement is published here, so treat that as the
  shape of the algorithm rather than a number
* the radius and angle maps (`:r_cylinder`, `:r_sphere`, `:ϕ`) exist only there, because they
  describe a pixel's own geometry and an off-axis pixel is a slanted column with no single
  value; an off-axis call asking for one is rejected rather than answered wrongly. Velocity
  dispersions are **not** in that group: the box-frame set (`:σx`, `:σy`, `:σz`, `:σ` and the
  cylindrical and spherical ones) works on both paths
* the off-axis path adds camera-frame kinematics the axis-aligned one cannot have: `:vlos` and
  `:σlos` along the line of sight, `:vcamx`/`:σcamx` and `:vcamy`/`:σcamy` along the image axes,
  and the `:ncell`/`:npart` counters
* the off-axis path has `fov`/`aperture` framing, which the axis-aligned one does not need

Particles have two paths as well, and they differ in more than speed: the axis-aligned one is a
plain histogram (so `binning` is not read, and empty pixels are `NaN`), while the off-axis one
deposits through the camera basis (empty pixels are `0.0`, `:overlap`/`:exact` fall back to
`:cic`, and `:npart` exists only there).

## Where the detail lives

* [Off-axis Projection](06_offaxis_Projection.md), the full treatment: camera, framing, accuracy,
  kinematics, slices, orbit movies, and what works on which data type
* [Hydro](06_hydro_Projection.md) and [Particles](06_particles_Projection.md), the axis-aligned
  tutorials
* [Pipelines](pipelines.md), projecting several quantities in one line and reusing one
  selection across loading and projection
* [Auto-Frame](galaxyframe.md), finding an object's own orientation
* [Movies](movie.md), assembling and writing them
* `projection()` with no arguments prints the whole keyword surface, which is the fastest way to
  find a keyword whose name you do not yet know


<!-- ===== offaxis_cheatsheet.md ===== -->

# Off-axis cheatsheet

Everything an off-axis projection can do, on one page. The
[Off-axis tutorial](06_offaxis_Projection.md) shows each item working, chapter by chapter.

Works the same on hydro and on particles unless a row says otherwise.

**A word used everywhere below: `los`, the line of sight.** It names the line through the object
that the camera looks along. The vector points from the object **toward the camera**: the camera
sits on the `+los` side and looks along `-los`, so `los=[0,0,1]` looks down from `+z`, like
`direction=:z`. A projection adds up everything along that line, so each pixel is the total (or
average) of one straight column through the data. "Off-axis" means the line of sight is not one of
the box axes x, y or z.

## Am I off-axis at all?

| call | path |
|---|---|
| `direction=:x`, `:y`, `:z` | **axis-aligned.** No camera is built. `m.los` is empty |
| `direction=:faceon`, `:edgeon` | off-axis |
| `los=`, `inclination=`, `azimuth=`, `theta=`/`phi=`, `position_angle=` | off-axis |

Some variables exist only on one path, so a call that silently took the other one gives a
confusing error. Check `m.los`: if it is empty, the camera was never built.

## Pointing the camera

Give **exactly one** line-of-sight specifier. If you give two, Mera raises an error.

| keyword | means |
|---|---|
| `los=[x,y,z]` | the line of sight, pointing toward the camera. Need not be a unit vector |
| `direction=:faceon` / `:edgeon` | derive the axis from the data's own angular momentum |
| `inclination=`, `azimuth=` | tilt away from a reference `axis` |
| `theta=`, `phi=` | deprecated since 1.8. Use `inclination`/`azimuth`; for `axis=:z`, `azimuth = phi + 90` |

And these modify whichever you chose:

| keyword | means |
|---|---|
| `up=[x,y,z]` | which way is up in the image |
| `position_angle=` | roll the image about the line of sight |
| `axis=` | the reference that `inclination`/`azimuth` tilt away from. Default `:z` |
| `angle_unit=:deg` (default) or `:rad` | how the angles are read |

### `axis=` takes

`:x`, `:y`, `:z`, a 3-vector `[ax,ay,az]`, or `:angmom` (alias `:L`) for the data's own angular
momentum. Combining `axis=` with `direction=:faceon`/`:edgeon` is an error, because those presets
already use `L`.

### How `los` becomes an image

Mera builds a right-handed orthonormal basis from `los`:

| returned on the map | is |
|---|---|
| `m.los` | the line of sight, normalised, pointing toward the camera |
| `m.cam_right` | image x, the map's first index |
| `m.up` | image y, the map's second index |

with `cam_right × up = los`, so `los` points out of the image toward you.

Without `up=`, the camera uses world **+z** as its up hint, falling back to +y when the line of
sight is within 3 degrees of the z axis. Along the six box directions this gives:

| `los` | image x | image y | compared with the axis-aligned map |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[0,0,1]` | `+x` | `+y` | the same orientation as `direction=:z` |
| `[0,0,-1]` | `-x` | `+y` | `direction=:z` mirrored left to right: seen from the other side |
| `[1,0,0]` | `+y` | `+z` | the same orientation as `direction=:x` |
| `[-1,0,0]` | `-y` | `+z` | `direction=:x` mirrored |
| `[0,-1,0]` | `+x` | `+z` | the same orientation as `direction=:y` |
| `[0,1,0]` | `-x` | `+z` | `direction=:y` mirrored |
| `[1,1,1]` | `(-x+y)/√2` | `(-x-y+2z)/√6` | no counterpart. Up is +z as seen across the line of sight |

"The same orientation" means the image axes agree. The pixel grids still differ slightly, because
the two paths place pixel edges differently, so do not subtract one map from the other.

Pass `up=` yourself whenever the default is not what you want. `position_angle` then rolls the
result about the line of sight without changing `m.los`.

**One rule, every spelling.** The same up rule is the reference for `inclination`/`azimuth` and
for `face_on`/`edge_on`, so these are identical views, not merely the same line of sight:

| | is exactly |
|---|---|
| `direction=:faceon` | `inclination=0, axis=:angmom` |
| `direction=:edgeon` | `inclination=90, azimuth=0, axis=:angmom` |

[`face_on`](@ref) and [`edge_on`](@ref) use the same camera rule, so their frames match the presets
when the angular momentum matches. They measure it about the centre of mass of the whole object
unless you give `center` or `aperture`, while the presets measure it about `center`, inside `fov`
and after `mask`. Pass a frame on as `los=fr.los, up=fr.up`.

Near the pole the up rule uses `+y` inside a 3 degree cone, so a face-on galaxy whose spin axis
wobbles by a hundredth of a degree keeps its roll. A spin axis that crosses the edge of the cone
between two snapshots still makes the image jump, so for a time series pass one fixed `axis=L` or
`up=`.

## Framing

| keyword | does |
|---|---|
| `fov=16`, `fov_unit=:kpc` | a fixed camera-plane window, the same at every angle. `fov_unit` defaults to `:standard`, a box fraction, so always give it |
| `fov=[wx, wy]` | a **rectangular** frame. Needs `aperture=:square` |
| `aperture=:circle` (default) / `:square` | `fov` is the radius of a disc, or the half-width of a square |
| `xrange`/`yrange`/`zrange`, `range_unit` | a world-space box. **Not** rotation invariant: tilting grows the frame and its faces show up as straight edges |
| `center` | what the window is about. With `fov` it is read in `fov_unit` and `range_unit` is ignored; without `fov` it is read in `range_unit` |
| `res=` or `pxsize=[v,:unit]` | how fine the pixels are. Prefer `pxsize` |

!!! warning "`center` defaults to the box corner"
    `projection` measures from `[0, 0, 0]`, not from the box centre. Always pass `center` with
    `fov`, `:faceon`, `:edgeon` or `axis=:angmom`, usually `center=[:bc]`; otherwise the `fov`
    sphere is an octant at the corner and the axis is measured about the corner. A centre taken
    from a map (`m.center`) or a `face_on` frame (`fr.center`) is a box fraction: do not pass it
    together with `fov_unit=:kpc`.

Without `fov`, an off-axis frame auto-fits the data it was given, so an object appears to zoom as
you rotate. `fov` is what stops that: the frame is then fixed by `fov`, symmetric about `center`
and the same at every angle, whether the data fills it or not. That holds for sparse data too, such
as a star disc, a masked selection or a thin `depth` slab. With `:circle`, a grid frame is one
coarse cell wider than `fov`, so a gas map and a star map share a pixel grid only with
`aperture=:square`.

`fov` is silently capped at `0.49·boxlen` for `:circle` and `0.49/√2·boxlen` for `:square`.

!!! note "A mask changes the frame"
    The camera extent is fitted to the cells that survive selection, so a masked map and an
    unmasked one do not share a pixel grid and cannot be divided one by the other. Pass `fov` to
    pin the window if you need to compare them.

## Cutting along the line of sight

| keyword | does |
|---|---|
| `depth=2`, `depth_unit=:kpc` | keep a slab of half-thickness 2 about `center`, measured **along the view** |
| `depth=[-2, 6]` | an explicit window, foreground and background need not match |
| particles: `thickness=2, thickness_unit=:kpc` | a slab of that depth along the view, moved with `offset`, `offset_unit`. The only line-of-sight cut on points |

`zrange` is world space and does not follow the camera; `depth` does. On an axis-aligned call the
line of sight **is** a box axis, so `zrange` already cuts this slab and `depth` is refused.

`fov` gives an uneven depth on its own: the sphere it selects is deepest on axis and reaches zero
at the frame boundary. `depth` is what makes the column the same length everywhere.

## Whole cells or partial ones

| | `split=false` (default) | `split=true` |
|---|---|---|
| `depth` slab | a cell is kept whole if its centre is inside | weighted by the fraction of its volume inside |
| `fov` sphere | a cell reaching the sphere is kept whole | weighted by its overlap fraction |

Use `split=true` when the edge matters: a small aperture, a thin slab, or **any time you stack
slabs and expect them to re-sum**. With whole cells, a cell on a cut is counted by both pieces. On
a regular grid a tilted line of sight can put many cell centres exactly on a cut, so the pieces add
up to more than the whole.

**`split=true` re-sums exactly: the pieces add up, and the map holds the mass of the split region.**
How wrong whole cells are depends entirely on your data. Both checks below come out at 0.0 percent
with `split=true`. Without it:

| check | Mera's test galaxy | the tutorial's 51.5 M cell snapshot |
|---|---|---|
| re-summing a partitioned slab | +4 % | +0.006 % |
| a small circular aperture | +7 % at 5 kpc | +0.45 % at 3 kpc |

The two differ by three orders of magnitude. The coarse test grid puts many cell centres exactly
on a face. The refined snapshot puts almost none there. And a 5 kpc aperture is a handful of coarse
cells across, but hundreds of fine ones. **Do not carry either number to your own run**: measure
it, as Chapter 5 of the [tutorial](06_offaxis_Projection.md) does.

!!! warning "`split`, `depth`, `refine` and `nmax` are grid-only"
    They are not keywords of the particle projection at all, so passing one is a
    `MethodError`, not a no-op. A point has no volume to split and no footprint to refine.

### Getting the mass right, and getting the edge sharp

These are two different jobs and they need two different keywords.

| | fixes | how |
|---|---|---|
| `split=true` | the **total** | a boundary cell contributes the fraction of its volume that is inside |
| `refine=N` / `refine_to=[l,:unit]` | **where the edge appears** | the boundary cells are octree-subdivided, so the boundary localises to `cellsize/2^N` and the rendered edge gets sharper |

`split` alone gives the right number with a staircase edge, because a half-in cell still deposits
its (reduced) mass over its whole footprint. `refine` cuts that cell into children so the mass
sits where it belongs. Both conserve: the total is unchanged by refining, it just moves.

```julia
projection(gas, :sd; center=[:bc], fov=5, fov_unit=:kpc, split=true, refine=2, los=[1,2,3])
```

`refine` needs `fov` and `split=true`, because it subdivides the cells the **sphere** crosses; it
raises otherwise. It does not apply to the `depth` slab, which is not a region.

Cost grows with the boundary area, at most `8^N` per boundary cell, so `refine=2` is usually
plenty and `refine_to` is the safer knob when the AMR level varies across the boundary.

The same two keywords exist on [`subregion`](@ref) for a region you select yourself, and that
`:fraction` column flows into off-axis maps too:

```julia
subregion(gas, sphere(10; center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc); split=true, refine=2)
```

!!! note "The region constructors are lowercase"
    `sphere`, `cylinder`, `cuboid`, `sphericalshell`, `cylindricalshell`. Makie exports a
    `Sphere` and a `Cylinder` too, and a name exported by two loaded packages binds to neither,
    so the capitalized types are no longer exported. They are still there as `Mera.Sphere` and
    so on if you need to dispatch on one.

## Choosing the axis from the data

| | |
|---|---|
| `angmom_radius=[10,:kpc]` | restrict the orientation sum to a sphere about `center` |
| [`angmom`](@ref)`(gas; center=[:bc], radius=[10,:kpc])` | the vector itself, to reuse |
| `angmom([gas, stars, dm]; ...)` | one axis from several components, momenta added |
| `angmom(gas; mask=cold)` | orient on part of the data (combines with `radius`) |
| [`face_on`](@ref) / [`edge_on`](@ref) | a frame; pass `los=fr.los, up=fr.up` to any call |

**What the presets measure.** `direction=:faceon`, `:edgeon` and `axis=:angmom` compute the axis
from **the data that gets drawn**, about `center`:

- These narrow the sum: `mask`, `parttypes`, the `fov` sphere (radius `fov`, or `√2·fov` for
  `aperture=:square`) and `angmom_radius`.
- These do not: `xrange`/`yrange`/`zrange` and `depth`. `depth` cannot, because it is measured
  along the axis being computed.
- Without `fov` or `angmom_radius` the sum runs over every cell or particle in the object. The
  outer material has the longest lever arm and can tilt a "face-on galaxy" by the halo. On
  particles that includes the dark matter, which usually dominates: pass `parttypes=[:stars]` or a
  mask to orient on the stars.

To orient on something other than what you draw, such as all components together, a selection
you do not want in the picture, or a fixed axis for a time series, compute the vector yourself and
pass it in. `projection` then uses it as given:

```julia
L = angmom([gas, stars, dm]; center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc, radius=[15, :kpc])
projection(gas, :sd; axis=L, inclination=0, center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc, mask=cold)
```

**The vector is per object.** Gas and stars each have their own, so `:faceon` on one is a
different camera from `:faceon` on the other. To compare them, compute one vector and pass it to
both:

```julia
L = angmom([gas, stars]; center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc, radius=[15, :kpc])
projection(gas,   :sd; axis=L, inclination=0, center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc)
projection(stars, :sd; axis=L, inclination=0, center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc)
```

The orientation is measured in the **box** velocity frame. For an object streaming through the
box, measuring about its own centre of mass largely cancels that, and `angmom(...; vcenter=:auto)`
removes the bulk motion outright.

## How a cell lands on the pixels

| `binning=` | what it does | cost |
|---|---|---|
| `:ngp` | the cell's centre picks one pixel | cheapest, blockiest |
| `:cic` | bilinear over a 2x2 stencil | cheap |
| `:overlap` (**grid default**) | splits the cell into `n³` sub-points, `n = ⌈cell/pixel⌉`, capped by `nmax=64` | accurate |
| `:exact` | analytic footprint | accurate, slowest |

Each kernel hands out the whole of every cell: the shares it gives to the pixels add up to one.
So all four keep the map total equal to the object's total, to rounding error. In tests the
difference is a few units of the last digit (`eps`), and at most about one part in 10¹² for
`:exact` with pixels much finer than the cells. The kernels differ in **where** the mass goes, not
in how much there is. This holds for extensive maps, the ones that add up: `:mass` and `:sd` on
cells, `:ekin`, `:etherm` and `:volume` with `mode=:sum`, `:sd` times the pixel area on particles,
and any particle quantity with `mode=:sum`. A mean such as `:T` does not sum to anything.

!!! warning "Two conditions, or the total is not the total"
    Every share must land on the grid, which the auto-fitted frame guarantees, and nothing
    may be cropped afterwards. `fov` with `aperture=:square` **does** crop, and how much it
    removes depends on the viewing angle, so never read a total off such a map. Check it:
    after `m = projection(obj, :sd, :Msol_pc2; ...)`, compare
    `sum(m.maps[:sd]) * (m.pixsize * m.scale.pc)^2` with `msum(obj, :Msol)`.

**On particles the default is `:cic`,** not `:overlap`. Points have no footprint, so `:overlap`
and `:exact` fall back to `:cic` and say so once. `nmax` does not exist there.

## Variables

### Available on any path

Almost everything `getvar` can produce: `:sd`, `:mass`, `:rho`, `:T`, `:vx`, the velocity
dispersions, and so on. The three exceptions are listed under **Axis-aligned only** below.

### Off-axis only

| | |
|---|---|
| `:vlos`, `:σlos` | along the line of sight. What a spectrum measures. Positive `:vlos` means moving away from the camera (redshift) |
| `:vcamx`, `:σcamx` | along image x |
| `:vcamy`, `:σcamy` | along image y |
| `:ncell` (hydro), `:npart` (particles) | how many fed each pixel |

Asked for on an axis-aligned call, these raise. The velocity ones name the box-frame equivalent.

### Axis-aligned only

`:r_cylinder`, `:r_sphere`, `:ϕ`. These describe the pixel's own geometry, and an off-axis pixel
is a slanted column with no single radius.

### σ against σ_LOS, v against v_LOS

This distinction is the reason there are two sets.

| | frame | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `:vz`, `:σz` | **box** axes. `:σz` is the spread along the simulation z | unchanged by where you put the camera |
| `:vlos`, `:σlos` | **camera**. Along the line of sight | changes when you move the camera |

Both work off-axis. `:σz` on a face-on view is still the simulation z, which is almost never what
a face-on view is asking about. The line-of-sight pair is the observable one: `:σlos` is the width
of the line a spectrograph would record. Edge-on, much of that width is rotation. `projection` has
no `vcenter`; to take the rotation out first, use `rotation_frame` and `restframe` (see
[How Quantities Are Computed](computation_reference.md)).

The full box-frame set is `:σx :σy :σz :σ :σr_cylinder :σϕ_cylinder :σr_sphere :σθ_sphere
:σϕ_sphere`, each built from its own `v` and `v²`.

!!! warning "`:σ` is not the tensor trace"
    `:σ` is the spread of the **speed**, `√(⟨|v|²⟩ − ⟨|v|⟩²)`. The trace of the dispersion tensor
    is `σx² + σy² + σz² = ⟨|v|²⟩ − |⟨v⟩|²`. They are different numbers, and `:σ` is the smaller
    one.

The camera triple and the box triple describe one tensor in two frames, so
`σcamx² + σcamy² + σlos² = σx² + σy² + σz²`, pixel by pixel.

### Counting what fed a pixel

`:ncell` and `:npart` ride along with any other variable and are filled by the same deposit.
What the number means depends on the kernel:

| `binning=` | the count is |
|---|---|
| `:ngp` | one per cell or particle. The map sums to exactly how many there were |
| `:cic` | one per pixel of the 2x2 stencil |
| `:overlap` | one per pixel each sub-point touches, so sampling density rather than an object tally |
| `:exact` | one per pixel the footprint covers |

Use it to find the pixels you cannot quote: a pixel holding one object has a dispersion of exactly
zero, and a mean that is just that one object.

## Weighting and totals

| keyword | values |
|---|---|
| `weighting=` (hydro) | `[:mass, unit]` (default), `[:volume, unit]`, or any getvar quantity |
| `weighting=` (particles) | `:mass` (default), `:volume`, `:sph`, `:voronoi` (see the note below) |
| `mode=` | `:standard`, a weighted mean Σq·w/Σw, or `:sum`: Σq·w on cells (a plain Σq only for `:ekin`, `:etherm`, `:volume`), a plain Σq on particles |

`:sd` and `:mass` on hydro are always summed; `mode` changes the other variables.

On particles `projection(part, :mass)` is the mass-weighted **mean particle mass**, because a
particle has no volume. For the mass in each pixel use `mode=:sum`, or `:sd` times the pixel area.

Dispersions are always built from weighted means, whatever `mode` says: a width is not a sum.
With `mode=:sum` the velocity components themselves (`:vx` and so on) are still sums.

!!! note "`:sph` and `:voronoi` need a size for each particle"
    `:sph` spreads each particle over a kernel set by its smoothing length, and `:voronoi` gives
    each pixel to the nearest particle, sized by its volume. `:voronoi` needs a `:volume` column,
    `:sph` a `:volume` column or a smoothing length (`:subfind_hsml`). RAMSES star and dark matter particles have neither, so on RAMSES data these
    two raise an error and `:mass` is the choice. They exist for moving-mesh and SPH gas (AREPO,
    GADGET), whose readers live on the `multicode` branch, where they are also illustrated.

## Masking

`mask=` takes one boolean per row of the object you pass.

```julia
cold = getvar(gas, :T, :K) .< 1e4
projection(gas, :sd; los=[1,2,3], mask=cold, center=[:bc], fov=16, fov_unit=:kpc)
```

It composes with `fov` everywhere, with `depth` and `split` on grid data, and with
`parttypes` on particles. It also sets the camera for `:faceon`, `:edgeon` and `axis=:angmom`:
`mask=cold` orients on the cold gas, and `parttypes=[:dm], direction=:faceon` on the dark matter
alone. Pass `axis=L` if the axis should come from other data.

For value-space selection, [`filterdata`](@ref) and [`getmask`](@ref) build masks from any getvar
quantity.

## Slices

A slice is not a projection. It is a nearest-cell painter on a plane: cells tile space, one owns
each pixel, and nothing is integrated or conserved.

```julia
sl = slice(gas, :rho, :g_cm3; los=[1,2,3], center=[:bc], pxsize=[0.5,:kpc])
```

| field | is |
|---|---|
| `sl.map` | the value, `NaN` where the plane painted nothing |
| `sl.coverage` | which pixels were painted |
| `sl.cellsize` | the size of the cell that won each pixel |
| `sl.depth` | how far the centre of that cell sits from the plane (`Inf` where nothing was painted) |

Slices work on cell data only (not particles), one variable at a time. `offset`/`offset_unit`
moves the plane along the view, and `xrange`/`yrange` set the window in the camera plane. There is
no `fov` and no `binning`. There is no cell count, because it would read 1 everywhere. `cellsize` against `pixsize` is the
useful diagnostic: where the cell is larger than the pixel, the extra pixels carry no extra
information.

## What comes back

| field | is |
|---|---|
| `m.maps[:var]` | the map |
| `m.maps_unit`, `m.maps_mode` | what each map is in, and how it was made |
| `m.maps_weight` | **grid maps only**; particle maps have no such field |
| `m.maps_lmax` | **always empty**, on every path. A leftover field, not a record |
| `m.center` | a **box fraction**, not a length. On grid maps your `center`, on particle maps the frame centre, empty on axis-aligned maps (a `slice` result's `.center` is code units) |
| `m.los`, `m.up`, `m.cam_right` | the camera that made it |
| `m.extent`, `getextent(m, :kpc)` | the frame, relative to the frame centre: `center` with `fov` or ranges, otherwise the centre of the loaded data |
| `m.pixsize`, `m.ratio` | pixel size and aspect |

Empty off-axis pixels are `0.0`, not `NaN`: filter on `> 0` before taking a logarithm or a
minimum.

Off-axis, `getextent` is measured from the frame centre. On the axis-aligned path it is absolute
box coordinates.

## Reproducing a map

A map carries what you need to make it again. [`provenance`](@ref)`(m)` records the snapshot and
the Mera build (path, output, time, levels, version and commit). The camera is on the map itself:
`m.los`, `m.up`, `m.cam_right`, `m.center`, `m.pixsize` and `m.extent`. [`savemap`](@ref) stores
both, so a map reloaded with [`loadmap`](@ref) still says where it came from and how it was made.

The one input that is not on the map is the data behind a `:faceon`, `:edgeon` or `axis=:angmom`
view. That axis depends on what you loaded, `center`, the `mask`, `parttypes`, `fov` and
`angmom_radius`. To repeat a view
exactly, reuse the recorded vectors instead of the preset:

```julia
projection(gas2, :sd; los=m.los, up=m.up, center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc, fov=16, fov_unit=:kpc)
```

For a time series, compute the axis once with [`angmom`](@ref) and pass it to every snapshot. See
also [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md).

## Movies, other data and periodic boxes

- **An orbit movie:** [`rotation_sequence`](@ref) sweeps `:azimuth`, `:inclination` or
  `:position_angle`. It defaults to `axis=:angmom` and, without `fov`, fits the frame to the radius
  that holds 99 % of the mass.
- **Gravity:** `projection(hydro, gravity, var)`. **Radiative transfer** has no velocities, so
  `:faceon`, `:edgeon` and `axis=:angmom` fail on it: pass `axis=angmom(gas; center=[:bc])`.
- **Periodic boxes:** an off-axis map cannot be rolled across the box, and
  [`periodic_recenter`](@ref) refuses it. Keep the object away from a box face (see
  [Periodic Boxes](periodic_boxes.md)).

## Things that will surprise you

- **A mask changes the picture size.** Without `fov`, the frame is fitted around the data that is
  left after the mask. Two maps with different masks then have different pixel grids. Give `fov`
  to fix the frame.
- **`fov` alone does not give equal depth.** `fov` selects a sphere, so a ray through the centre of
  the frame is long and a ray near the edge is short. Add `depth` if every pixel should look
  through the same thickness.
- **`:σz` is always the simulation's z direction,** also in a face-on view. The spread you would
  measure with a telescope is `:σlos`.
- **`:σ` is not the total spread.** It is the spread of the speed. For the total, take
  `√(σx² + σy² + σz²)`.
- **Thin slabs with whole cells do not add up** to the thick slab they were cut from, because a
  cell on a boundary is counted in both. Use `split=true`.
- **Gas and stars give different `:faceon` views,** because each rotates about its own axis.
  Compute one axis with `angmom` and pass it to both.
- **`direction=:x`, `:y` and `:z` are not off-axis.** The camera-only variables such as `:vlos`
  are refused there. Use `los=[0,0,1]` to get the camera path along a box axis.


<!-- ===== subregions_cheatsheet.md ===== -->

# Subregions cheatsheet

Everything `subregion` and `shellregion` can do, on one page. The
[Get Subregions tutorial](03_hydro_Get_Subregions.md) shows each item working, step by step.

| function | cuts |
|---|---|
| `subregion` | a solid shape: box, cylinder or sphere. With a region value also a shell, and any combination of shapes |
| `shellregion` | a hollow shell: spherical, or cylindrical (a ring of finite height) |

Works the same on hydro, gravity and RT data. Particles, clumps and sinks are points; the rows
below say where that changes something.

## Two ways to write a region

| | region value | classic symbol |
|---|---|---|
| call | `subregion(gas, sphere(10.))` | `subregion(gas, :sphere; radius=10.)` |
| shells | `subregion(gas, sphericalshell(10., 20.))` | `shellregion(gas, :sphere; radius=[10., 20.])` |
| default centre | box centre, `[:bc]` | box **corner**, `[0., 0., 0.]` |
| default unit | `:kpc` | `:standard` (code units) |
| boundary cells | split, with a `:fraction` per cell | whole cells (`cell=true`) or centre test (`cell=false`) |
| combine with `∩ ∪ \ !` | yes | no |
| tilt (cylinder, cylindrical shell) | yes, `axis=[x, y, z]` | no, along z only |
| wrap at periodic faces | no | yes, `periodic=true` |

Use region values to measure. Use the classic form for quick looks, for periodic runs, and in
older scripts.

## `subregion` and `shellregion`

Both work on every data type and return the same type as their input. `shellregion` takes the
same classic keywords as `subregion`: `center`, `range_unit`, `cell`, `inverse`, `periodic`,
`verbose` and `myargs`. A shell can be cut three ways:

```julia
subregion(gas, sphericalshell(10., 20.))      # region value: boundary cells split
subregion(gas, sphere(20.) \ sphere(10.))     # the same shell as a difference, same sampling accuracy
shellregion(gas, :sphere; radius=[10., 20.],  # classic: whole cells or centre test
            center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc)
```

The cylindrical shell in the same three forms:

```julia
subregion(gas, cylindricalshell(6., 10., 2.))                 # inner radius, outer radius, half-height
subregion(gas, cylinder(10., 2.) \ cylinder(6., 2.))
shellregion(gas, :cylinder; radius=[6., 10.], height=2., center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc)
```

### Shell rules

- `radius=[r_in, r_out]`: inner radius first. In `shellregion` both must be larger than zero;
  for a full ball use a sphere.
- `height` of a cylindrical shell is the half-height, as for the cylinder. The classic
  cylindrical shell runs along z only; `cylindricalshell(…; axis=[x, y, z])` tilts it.
- `shellregion(obj)` without a shape means `:cylinder`. Name the shape to be safe.
- `inverse=true` selects everything outside the shell: the inside of `r_in` together with the
  outside of `r_out`.
- A shell has two surfaces. With `cell=true` the classic shell keeps every cell that touches
  it, on both surfaces, like every other classic shape: its mass is an upper bound. With
  `cell=false` the centre test applies on both surfaces. `sphericalshell` and
  `cylindricalshell` split the cells of both surfaces.
- **Nested classic shells overlap with `cell=true`**: neighbours share the cells on their common
  edge, so a radial profile from them counts those cells twice. Use `cell=false` (each cell goes
  to one shell) or region values (each cell is split between the shells).
- A shell and the sphere (or cylinder) inside it share the inner surface. With region values
  their masses add up exactly to the mass of the outer sphere.
- `periodic=true` works with `shellregion`, as with `subregion`.

## Shapes

| shape | region value | classic call | tilt |
|---|---|---|---|
| box | `cuboid(xrange=[a,b], yrange=[c,d], zrange=[e,f])` | `subregion(obj, :cuboid; xrange=, yrange=, zrange=)` | no, aligned with the axes |
| cylinder | `cylinder(r, h)` | `subregion(obj, :cylinder; radius=r, height=h)` | region value: `axis=[x, y, z]`; classic: along z only |
| sphere | `sphere(r)` | `subregion(obj, :sphere; radius=r)` | not needed |
| spherical shell | `sphericalshell(r_in, r_out)` | `shellregion(obj, :sphere; radius=[r_in, r_out])` | not needed |
| cylindrical shell | `cylindricalshell(r_in, r_out, h)` | `shellregion(obj, :cylinder; radius=[r_in, r_out], height=h)` | region value: `axis=[x, y, z]`; classic: along z only |

- **`h` is the half-height.** `cylinder(12., 2.)` spans z from −2 to +2, so it is 4 kpc thick.
  The classic `height=` means the same.
- Box ranges are measured from `center`. In the classic `:cuboid`, a range left out (or
  `[0, 0]`) means the full box along that axis.
- **Tilt.** `cylinder` and `cylindricalshell` take `axis=[x, y, z]`, any non-zero vector, and
  then run along that direction: a disc tilted like the galaxy, a bar in the disc plane, a ring
  seen at an angle. The axis also works inside combinations. A sphere and a spherical shell look
  the same in every direction, and the box is always aligned with the axes. The classic
  `:cylinder` and `shellregion(:cylinder)` run along z only; another `direction` is an error.
- The classic `:disc` is another name for `:cylinder`.

## Placing a region

| `center=` | means |
|---|---|
| `[:bc]` or `[:boxcenter]` | the box centre |
| `[x, y, z]` | a point, in `range_unit`, measured from the box corner |
| `[13., :bc, :bc]` | mixed: x = 13, box centre in y and z |
| `collect(center_of_mass(gas, :kpc))` | a point taken from the data |

`range_unit=` is the unit of the centre and of every size: `:kpc`, `:pc`, `:Mpc`, `:au`, … or
`:standard` for code units. `info.scale` lists them all.

A classic sphere, cylinder or shell without `center` sits on the box corner and keeps only the
part inside the box. Mera prints a note once per shape when this happens.

## Boundary cells

Only cell data (hydro, gravity, RT) have boundary cells. Particles, clumps and sinks are in or out.

| treatment | how to ask | the mass you get |
|---|---|---|
| split | region value, default `split=true` | exact, to the sampling accuracy of `nsub` |
| centre test | `split=false`, or classic `cell=false` | an estimate; can be too high or too low |
| whole cells | classic `cell=true` (the classic default) | always too high: an upper bound |

With `split=true` each kept cell carries `:fraction ∈ (0, 1]`, the part of its volume inside the
region.

| keyword (region values) | default | does |
|---|---|---|
| `nsub` | `8` | points per axis used to measure the fraction of a cell cut by a curved surface. A box aligned with the axes is computed exactly |
| `refine` | `0` | replace boundary cells by their children, down to `refine` levels. Sharper edge in maps, same numbers |
| `refine_to` | `nothing` | `[length, unit]`: each boundary cell picks its own depth so its children are no larger than this. Set it to the map's `pxsize`. Not together with `refine` |

The errors of whole cells and of the centre test grow with the size of the cells at the
boundary. A small region, or one far from the refined gas, can be off by a large factor.

### What the fraction scales

Quantities that say **how much**: `:mass`, `:volume`, and energies built from them. They are
multiplied by the fraction in `getvar`, `msum` and projections. Quantities that say **what the
gas is like** keep their value: density, temperature, velocity, potential. Details:
[Subregions API](api/subregions.md#What-the-fraction-is-applied-to).

## Inside and outside

| call | selects |
|---|---|
| `subregion(obj, region; inverse=true)` | everything outside |
| `shellregion(obj, :sphere; radius=[r_in, r_out], inverse=true)` | everything outside the shell |
| `subregion(obj, !region)` | the same, written into the region |
| classic `inverse=true` | the same, for classic calls |

The fractions flip (`1 − fraction`), so a region and its inverse add up to the whole box.

## Combining regions

| operator | ASCII form | function | selects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A ∩ B` | `A & B` | `intersect(A, B)` | inside both |
| `A ∪ B` | `A \| B` | `union(A, B)` | inside at least one |
| `A \ B` | | `setdiff(A, B)` | inside A, not inside B |
| `!A` | | | outside A |

Each part can have its own centre, and combinations nest freely. Type `∪` as `\cup` TAB and `∩`
as `\cap` TAB.

```julia
shape = @region unit=:kpc center=[:bc] begin
    disc    = cylinder(12., 2.)
    blister = sphere(2.5; center=[30., :bc, 26.])     # an explicit keyword wins
    chimney = cylinder(1.2, 5.; center=[19., :bc, :bc])
    (disc ∪ blister) \ chimney
end
subregion(gas, shape)
```

Inside `@region`, every constructor that does not set `center`/`range_unit` gets the block's
values. The result is an ordinary region.

**Cutting a cut.** `subregion` on an object that was already split multiplies the fractions.
That is exact unless one cell is cut by both surfaces; Mera then prints a hint. For the exact
result use `subregion(obj, region1 ∩ region2)`.

## Classic keywords

```julia
subregion(obj, :cuboid | :cylinder | :sphere;
          xrange, yrange, zrange,          # cuboid, measured from center
          radius, height,                  # cylinder (half-height), sphere
          center=[0., 0., 0.], range_unit=:standard,
          cell=true, inverse=false, periodic=false, verbose=true, myargs)

shellregion(obj, :cylinder | :sphere;
            radius=[r_in, r_out], height,  # height for the cylinder
            center=[0., 0., 0.], range_unit=:standard,
            cell=true, inverse=false, periodic=false, verbose=true, myargs)
```

`myargs=ArgumentsType(...)` passes a bundle of keywords at once, see
[Bundled Arguments](bundled_arguments.md). Radii and heights must be larger than zero.

## Periodic boxes

| | |
|---|---|
| `periodic=true` | the classic region wraps around all box faces |
| `periodic=(x=true, y=true, z=false)` | wraps only some axes |
| cylinders | wrap in their two radial directions, never along the height |
| region values | never wrap; they are clipped at the faces |
| `info.boundaries` | `:periodic`, `:nonperiodic` or `:unknown`, read from the namelist |

Mera never wraps on its own: RAMSES does not store the boundary conditions in its output. See
[Periodic Boxes](periodic_boxes.md) for `:r_sphere_periodic`, `center_of_mass(…; periodic=true)`
and `periodic_recenter`.

## Data types

| data | region values | classic | boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| hydro, gravity, RT | yes | yes | split, centre test, or whole cells |
| particles | yes | yes | point in or out |
| clumps | yes | yes | point at the clump's peak position |
| sinks | yes | yes | point in or out |

For points, `cell=` has no effect (`cell=false` prints a warning). `split=true` on RAMSES particles is an error:
particles have no volume to split.

!!! tip "Gravity energies: cut the hydro object the same way"
    `getvar(grav, gas, :total_binding_energy)` and similar take their mass from the hydro object,
    so cut both with the same region: `subregion(grav, R)` and `subregion(gas, R)`. Mera refuses
    a hydro object that was cut differently.

## The result

- The same type as the input: `msum`, `getvar`, `projection`, `profile`, `savedata` and another
  `subregion` work on it unchanged.
- `Mera.select(cut.data, :fraction)` reads the fractions of a split cut.
- `Mera.get_filtered_ranges(cut)` returns the bounding ranges of a classic cut, normalised to the
  box, ready for `projection`.
- `savedata(cut, path)` stores a cut; `loaddata` reads it back. Cut before saving: `loaddata`
  reads the whole file.

## Traps

1. **The cylinder height is a half-height.** `cylinder(r, 2.)` is 4 units thick.
2. **The classic default centre is the box corner**, and the classic default unit is code units.
3. **Region values do not wrap** at periodic faces. Use the classic call with `periodic=true`.
4. **The centre test is not a bound.** Only whole cells give a guaranteed upper limit, and only
   the split cut gives the measurement.
5. **Whole-cell regions that touch overlap.** Neighbouring classic shells, or a classic sphere
   and the shell around it, share the cells on their common surface. For a budget or a profile,
   use region values or `cell=false`.
6. **A hole is hard to see** in a projection through the whole box: the line of sight still
   passes the gas in front of and behind it. Limit the depth, e.g. `zrange=` of the region.
7. **A split edge looks soft in a map**, because each cut cell is drawn over its full size. The
   numbers are right; use `refine` or `refine_to` for the picture.
8. **A cut of a cut** multiplies the fractions. Combine the regions with `∩` for the exact joint
   fraction.

## Related

| you want to | see |
|---|---|
| select by value: density, temperature, any `getvar` field | [Masking & Filtering](05_multi_Masking_Filtering.md), `filterdata`, `getmask` |
| distances in a periodic box | `getvar(obj, :r_sphere_periodic; center=…)` |
| look along a tilted region's axis | [Off-axis projection](06_offaxis_Projection.md) |
| a uniform grid of a region | [Covering Grid](covering_grid.md) |


<!-- ===== profiles_phase.md ===== -->

# Profiles & Phase Diagrams

!!! tip "Step-by-step tutorial"
    For a runnable walk-through (radial/vertical profiles, per-bin statistics, mass vs volume
    weighting, stars/gravity, profiles from 2-D maps, phase diagrams): see the
    [Profiles & phase diagrams tutorial](15_multi_Profiles_Phase.md).

`profile` and `phase` are **general weighted reductions** over any `getvar` fields: they are not
tied to projection or to a line of sight. A *profile* bins the data by one field; a *phase
diagram* is a 2D weighted histogram of two fields. They work on

* **3D data**: hydro, gravity, particles and clumps, using each type's available fields. (Gravity
  carries no `:mass`, so weight by `:volume`/`:none`; clumps expose only their stored columns,
  `:mass`, `:peak_x/y/z`, `:rho_av`, …, not derived coordinates like `:r_cylinder`.)
* **projected 2D maps**: a [`projection`](@ref) result, via `profile(m::DataMapsType, …)` /
  `phase(m::DataMapsType, …)` (the returns carry `source=:map`); see the tutorial.

Over the **full data range** (the default `xrange`) the binned weights sum to the grand total, e.g.
a radial mass profile sums to the total mass. Restricting `xrange`/`edges` instead sums only the
weight **inside that range**.

![Rotation curve, enclosed-mass profile and a mass-weighted density-temperature phase diagram](assets/analysis/profiles_phase.png)

## What you can compute

A profile is configurable along a few **independent** axes: mix and match freely.

**Data source**: 3-D data (`profile(obj, …)`) or a projected 2-D map (`profile(m::DataMapsType, …)`).

**Per-bin reduction**: with a `yvar`, every bin returns *all* of these at once:

| reduction | field(s) | notes |
|---|---|---|
| count / summed weight | `count`, `sum`, `sumw2` | always returned; `sum` = Σweight (the mass/volume/… profile) |
| weighted mean | `mean` | |
| standard deviation | `std` | weight-weighted |
| standard error of the mean | `sem`, `neff` | `sem = std/√neff` (Kish effective sample size) |
| median & **percentiles** | `median`, `quantiles`, `qlevels` | weighted; set the levels via `quantiles=[…]` |
| **extrema** | `min`, `max` | |
| **shape moments** | `skewness`, `kurtosis` | weighted; `kurtosis` is **excess** (0 for a Gaussian) |
| custom | `custom` | `statistic = f(yview, wview)` (or `f(yview)`) |

**Weighting**: `weight = :mass` · `:volume` (grid only) · `:none` (equal cells) · any field. (Should
be non-negative.)
**Binning**: `nbins` + `xrange` + `scale=:linear`/`:log`/**`:equal`** (quantile-spaced *adaptive*
bins, ~equal count per bin, robust for sparse outer radii / noisy data), or explicit `edges=[…]`.
`:log` is **base 10**, not natural log: the edges are `10 .^ range(log10(lo), log10(hi), …)`, so a
`binsize` under `:log` is a dimensionless **dex** step (0.1 = ten bins per decade). The same holds
for `xscale`/`yscale`/`zscale` in `phase` and `profile3d`. Values ≤ 0 have no log bin and are
dropped with a warning.
**Reference point**: `center` in `center_unit` (e.g. `center=[24,24,24], center_unit=:kpc`); the
binning-axis unit is `xunit`, **not** `center_unit` (the axis can be any quantity). `range_unit` is
a back-compat alias of `center_unit`.

**One-line transforms** (opt-in):

| want | kwarg | adds |
|---|---|---|
| physical density ρ(r) / Σ(R) | `geometry=:spherical` / `:cylindrical` | `shell_volume`, `density` |
| **cumulative** / enclosed M(<r) | `cumulative=:forward` / `:reverse` | `cumsum`, `cumcount` |
| normalized histogram (fractions / **PDF**) | `normalize=:sum` / `:pdf` | `fraction`, `pdf` |
| **bootstrap uncertainties** | `bootstrap=N` (`ci=:percentile`/`:basic`/`:bca`) | `mean_ci`, `median_ci` (`nbins×2`), `median_se` |
| **several fields in one pass** | `yvar = [:a, :b]` | `fields[:a]`, `fields[:b]`, `yvars` |

**Normalizations: fractions, PDFs & density PDFs.** With no `yvar`, the binned `sum` is a histogram
of `weight`; `normalize=:sum` → `fraction = sum/Σsum` (bins add to 1); `normalize=:pdf` →
`pdf = fraction/Δedge` (a true probability density, ∫ = 1, bin-width independent). The classic case is
the **density PDF**, bin *by* `:rho` and normalize; `weight=:mass` vs `:volume` give the mass- vs
volume-weighted ρ-PDF. The same `normalize=:pdf` makes a 2-D PDF in `phase` and a 3-D PDF in
`profile3d`. *(Worked, plotted example: tutorial §3.)*

**Bin widths by count, physical size, or population.** Set bins by **count** (`nbins`+`xrange`),
**physical width** (`binsize`), or explicit `edges`:

| you want | pass | note |
|---|---|---|
| `n` bins over a range | `nbins=40, xrange=(0,20)` | default |
| a fixed width Δ (in `xunit`) | `binsize=0.5` | e.g. 0.5-kpc radial bins; overrides `nbins` |
| a width with its own unit | `binsize=(500,:pc)` | converted to `xunit`; final bin may be short (keeps the top edge) |
| a fixed **dex** step (log) | `scale=:log, binsize=0.25` | log10-spaced; `binsize` is a dimensionless dex step |
| ~equal points per bin | `scale=:equal` | quantile-spaced adaptive bins (no `binsize`) |
| exact edges | `edges=[…]` | in `xunit`; wins over everything |

(`phase`/`profile3d` take per-axis `xbinsize`/`ybinsize`/`zbinsize`.)

### Result fields: quick reference

What a `profile` returns (a `NamedTuple`; only the relevant fields are present):

| field(s) | shape | when |
|---|---|---|
| `x`, `edges`, `count`, `sum`, `sumw2` | `nbins` (`edges`: `nbins+1`) | **always** (`sum` = Σweight) |
| `mean`, `std`, `var`, `sem`, `neff`, `min`, `max`, `median`, `skewness`, `kurtosis` | `nbins` | with a `yvar` |
| `quantiles`, `qlevels` | `nbins×nq`, `nq` | with a `yvar` |
| `shell_volume`, `density` | `nbins` | `geometry=:spherical`/`:cylindrical` |
| `cumsum`, `cumcount` | `nbins` | `cumulative=:forward`/`:reverse` |
| `fraction` (`+ pdf`) | `nbins` | `normalize=:sum` (`:pdf`) |
| `mean_ci`, `median_ci`, `median_se`, `ci_level`, `ci_method`, `nboot` | `nbins×2` / `nbins` | `bootstrap=N` |
| `custom` | `nbins` | `statistic=f` |
| `fields[:name]`, `yvars` | per field | vector `yvar` (each field nests the per-bin stats above) |
| `weight`, `xvar`, `yvar`, `xunit`, `unit`, `source` |, | provenance (`weight=:vector` for a raw-vector weight) |

### Choosing the tool

| tool | bins | output | per-bin value | typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `profile(obj, x[, y])` | 1 | `nbins` | Σweight, or stats of `y` | radial ρ(r), rotation curve, ⟨T⟩(r), PDFs |
| `phase(obj, x, y[, c])` | 2 | `nbins²` (`H`) | joint Σweight; `cstat` of `c` | ρ-T diagram, joint PDF |
| `profile3d(obj, x, y, z[, c])` | 3 | `nbins³` (`H`) | joint Σweight; `cstat` of `c` | ρ-T-Z cube; marginal ≡ `phase` |
| `velocitydispersion(obj)` | 1 (radius) | `nbins` | σ_R/σ_φ/σ_z + total σ | kinematic dispersion profile |
| `profiletimeseries(loadfn, outs, …)` | 1 × snapshots | `nbins×nsnap` | a profile per snapshot | radius-vs-time evolution |

!!! note "Conditional vs joint, `profile` vs `phase`"
    `profile(gas, :rho, :T)` is the **conditional** ⟨T⟩(ρ), one curve, the mean of `T` *given* ρ.
    `phase(gas, :rho, :T)` is the **joint** distribution `H[ρ,T]`. They agree at the margin:
    `sum(phase.H, dims=2)` equals `profile(gas, :rho).sum` on the same x-edges.

### Velocity dispersion

The per-bin `std` of a velocity *component* is already its **rest-frame** kinematic dispersion
(weighted variance about the per-bin mean, net rotation/streaming does **not** inflate it), so
`profile(gas, :r_cylinder, :vz).std` is σ_z(R), `…, :vϕ_cylinder).std` is σ_φ(R), etc.
[`velocitydispersion`](@ref) is a convenience wrapper that returns σ_R / σ_φ / σ_z (cylindrical by
default) and the total σ = √(σ_R²+σ_φ²+σ_z²) in one call.
*(Worked example: the tutorial's "More features" section.)*

#### Turbulent ⊕ thermal = total line width

The σ above is the **turbulent** (bulk) motion only. The width a spectrograph actually measures also
includes the gas **thermal** motion. Pass `thermal=true` (with `mu`, the tracer mean molecular weight
in H-atom masses: `2.33` molecular, `1.0` atomic, `0.6` ionized) to also get, per bin, the 1-D
turbulent `sigma_turb_1d = √(Σσ_i²/n)`, the thermal speed `sigma_thermal = √(k_B⟨T⟩/(μ m_H))`, the
**total** `sigma_total = √(sigma_turb_1d² + sigma_thermal²)`, and the turbulent Mach number
`mach = sigma_turb_1d/⟨c_s⟩`:

```julia
vt = velocitydispersion(gas; thermal=true, mu=2.33, nbins=20, xrange=(0,18), center=[:bc], center_unit=:kpc)
vt.sigma_total      # √(turbulent² + thermal²)  [km/s]
vt.mach             # σ_turb,1D / c_s
```

#### Local (patch-de-streamed) dispersion: [`localdispersion`](@ref)

`velocitydispersion` removes the mean per *radial bin*, so a velocity gradient across a wide annulus
(shear, spiral streaming) leaks into "turbulence". [`localdispersion`](@ref) instead tiles the (x, y)
plane into square `patchsize` patches and removes the **per-patch** mean velocity, the TIGRESS/SILCC
way to isolate turbulence below a chosen length scale. Restrict the input first (e.g. [`shellregion`](@ref)
to an annulus), it returns aggregate scalars over the supplied region, with the turbulent/thermal/total
σ, Mach, anisotropy, and the patch-to-patch percentile spread (usable as error bars):

```julia
solar = shellregion(gas, :cylinder, radius=[7,9], height=2, center=[:bc], range_unit=:kpc)
ld = localdispersion(solar; patchsize=[500,:pc], thermal=true, mu=2.33)
ld.sigma_total, ld.mach, ld.anisotropy, ld.sigma_total_q   # scalars + (16,50,84)% patch spread
```

!!! note "A rotation curve carries a sign"
    The binned mean azimuthal velocity, `profile(gas, :r_cylinder, :vϕ_cylinder)`, keeps the disk's
    **rotation sense**, so it can be **negative** (this galaxy's ⟨v_ϕ⟩ ≈ −230…−100 km/s). Plot
    `abs.(mean)` if you want a positive curve. For the curve set by the mass rather than by the gas
    motion, take it from the solved gravity field: `v = √(R·|a_R|)` with
    `getvar(grav, :ar_cylinder)`, which needs no assumption about how the mass is arranged.

## Profiles from 2-D maps

`profile(m::DataMapsType, var; xvar=:r, …)` bins the pixels of a [`projection`](@ref) result: a
surface-brightness Σ(R), a column-weighted `vlos(R)` (`weight=:sd`), a σlos(R), or any map vs any map.
It works for axis-aligned **and off-axis** maps: `xvar=:r` measures radius from the **object centre**
(the map's `cextent`/pivot), so the profile is correctly centred for asymmetric FOVs and off-axis
views; pass `center=[cx,cy]` (camera-plane, in `center_unit`) to offset it.
*(Worked examples, including off-axis: the tutorial's "More features" section.)*

These are box-axis / camera-independent reductions; for line-of-sight distributions (per-pixel
spectra, velocity cubes) see the [Off-axis Projection](06_offaxis_Projection.md) guide.

## API

```@docs; canonical=false
profile
phase
profile3d
velocitydispersion
localdispersion
profiletimeseries
getparticlemask
```

# Derived Fields & `add_field`

!!! tip "Run it yourself"
    This page is also an executable **Jupyter notebook**: [open / download `derived_fields.ipynb`](https://github.com/ManuelBehrendt/Notebooks/blob/master/Mera-Docs/version_1.1/derived_fields.ipynb). The notebooks run end-to-end and double as part of Mera's test suite.


Mera computes a large catalogue of **derived quantities** on demand through
[`getvar`](@ref), temperature, sound speed, Mach number, cylindrical/spherical velocities,
specific angular momentum, Jeans length, kinetic/thermal energy, and many more. You ask for
them by name and Mera builds them from the raw stored variables:

```julia
# Example-data root. Point this at your own simulation folder, or set the
# MERA_EXAMPLES environment variable; every path below is built from it.
MERA_EXAMPLES = get(ENV, "MERA_EXAMPLES", "/Volumes/FASTStorage/Simulations/Mera-Tests");

using Mera
info = getinfo(300, joinpath(MERA_EXAMPLES, "RAMSES/mw_L10"))
gas  = gethydro(info, verbose=false);
```

```

```

These derived names also work everywhere `getvar` is used internally, in
[`projection`](@ref), [`profile`](@ref), [`phase`](@ref), and friends.

!!! tip "Exact formulas"
    For the full set of formulas behind every derived quantity (thermodynamics, velocities,
    angular momentum, Mach numbers, Jeans/collapse, gravity) and the aggregate statistics
    (`msum`, `center_of_mass`, `bulk_velocity`, `wstat`), see
    [How Quantities Are Computed](computation_reference.md).

## Conventions for selected quantities

A few derived quantities carry physical assumptions worth stating explicitly:

- **Jeans length** `:jeanslength` uses the standard form ``λ_J = c_s\,\sqrt{\dfrac{3π}{32\,G\,ρ}}`` (and
  `:jeansmass`/`:jeansnumber` follow from it). This is one of several Jeans-length conventions in the
  literature; factors of order unity differ between them. The classical ``λ_J = \sqrt{π c^2/(Gρ)}`` is
  available with the isothermal (`:jeanslength_iso`, ``c^2=P/ρ``) or adiabatic (`:jeanslength_ad`,
  ``c^2=γP/ρ``) sound speed. The matching cells-per-Jeans-length are `:jeansnumber_iso`/`:jeansnumber_ad`,
  and `:jeansnumber_truelove` gives Truelove et al.'s (1997) ``J = Δx/λ_{J,\mathrm{iso}}``. The `_iso`
  variants are what RAMSES `jeans_refine` uses.
- **Magnetosonic Mach numbers** `:mach_alfven`, `:mach_fast`, `:mach_slow` require the magnetic-field
  components `:bx,:by,:bz` (an MHD run) and error otherwise. The B field is taken in **RAMSES code
  units** and converted to Gaussian-CGS internally (Alfvén speed ``v_A = B/\sqrt{4πρ}``); fast/slow use
  ``v_{f}=\sqrt{c_s^2+v_A^2}`` and the isotropic ``v_{s}=c_s v_A/\sqrt{c_s^2+v_A^2}``. All three are
  dimensionless. (Because they need the field components, `getvar_requirements` lists `:bx,:by,:bz,:rho`
  among their dependencies.)
- **Gravity energy and force** `:gravitational_energy`, `:total_binding_energy`, `:Fg` and the
  `:F…` components are mass times a gravity field, so they need the hydro object for the cell
  mass: `getvar(gravity, hydro, :Fg)`. On gravity alone they raise an error naming the fix.
- **Cosmological-only** quantities, `:overdensity`/`:delta` (hydro) and `:age`-relatives
  `:formation_time`/`:formation_redshift`/`:zform` (particles), are defined only for cosmological runs
  and error on non-cosmological output.

## The dependency registry

Each derived quantity knows which **raw** variables it is built from. That graph is queryable:

```julia
println("T [K] range           : ", extrema(getvar(gas, :T, :K)))
println("Mach range            : ", extrema(getvar(gas, :mach)))
println("ekin [erg] (sum)      : ", sum(getvar(gas, :ekin, :erg)))
println("requirements :ekin    : ", getvar_requirements(:hydro, :ekin))
println("requirements [:sd,:T] : ", getvar_requirements(:hydro, [:sd, :T]))
```

```
T [K] range           : (10.195354771220304, 2.3032126579487386e8)
[Mera] Hint: getvar(:v) has no `vcenter` — velocities are in the BOX frame.
             Pass vcenter=:auto for an object with bulk motion (`center=` sets the origin,
             `vcenter=` the frame). On a halo streaming at ~200 km/s this shifted |J| by 34 %.
             (shown once per session; verbose(false) silences Mera's messages)
Mach range            : (0.0015019848658968961, 790.5001832586903)
ekin [erg] (sum)      : 3.445146674042365e57
requirements :ekin    : [:rho, :vx, :vy, :vz]
requirements [:sd,:T] : [:p, :rho]
```

This is what lets the one-call verbs read **only what they need** instead of the whole hydro
state. `project(info, :sd)` reads just `:rho`; `project(info, :sd; direction=:edgeon)` also
pulls the velocities required to orient the disk; [`quicklook`](@ref) reads only `:rho` and
`:p`. When a requirement cannot be resolved (e.g. a custom field whose dependency is not
stored in that output) the readers safely fall back to reading everything.

## Adding your own field: `add_field`

Register a custom derived field once and it behaves like any built-in quantity, including
inside `projection` and `profile`.

```julia
add_field(:vmag2, (obj, deps) -> deps[:vx].^2 .+ deps[:vy].^2 .+ deps[:vz].^2;
          depends_on = [:vx, :vy, :vz])

println(":vmag2 via getvar     : ", extrema(getvar(gas, :vmag2)))
m = projection(gas, :vmag2; verbose=false)         # works in projection too
println(":vmag2 projection map : ", size(m.maps[:vmag2]))
```

```
:vmag2 via getvar     : (9.736562820569741e-6, 371.6168616499286)
:vmag2 projection map : (1024, 1024)
```

### The compute kernel

`compute(dataobject, deps)`:

* `dataobject`, the data object the field is being evaluated on.
* `deps`, a `Dict{Symbol,Vector}` holding the arrays named in `depends_on`, already
  evaluated with the **same** centering and masking as the outer `getvar` call.
* **Return** the field in **code units**; Mera applies the requested `unit` (or this field's
  default `unit`) for you.

Dependencies may be raw variables, other built-in derived quantities, or even other user
fields, they are resolved recursively:

```julia
add_field(:mach_custom, (o, d) -> sqrt.(d[:vx].^2 .+ d[:vy].^2 .+ d[:vz].^2) ./ d[:cs];
          depends_on = [:vx, :vy, :vz, :cs])
println(":mach_custom range    : ", extrema(getvar(gas, :mach_custom)))
```

```
:mach_custom range    : (0.0015019848658968961, 790.5001832586903)
```

A registered field is a first-class citizen: it flows through [`getvar`](@ref), [`projection`](@ref),
[`profile`](@ref) and the rest, with its dependencies read and resolved automatically. For example,
once `:mach_custom` is registered, `projection(gas, :mach_custom)` just works:

![A user-defined field projected like any built-in. `add_field(:mach_custom, …)` registers the local
Mach number ℳ = |v|/c_s on top of the built-in sound speed `:cs`; `projection(gas, :mach_custom)` then
renders it, supersonic disk gas (red) over the subsonic halo (blue).](assets/features/derived_fields.png)

### Units

Give a field a default `unit` (it must be a field of `info.scale`, or `:standard` for code
units). A unit passed at call time overrides the default:

```julia
add_field(:rho_msun_pc3, (o, d) -> d[:rho]; depends_on = [:rho], unit = :Msol_pc3)
getvar(gas, :rho_msun_pc3)               # returns code-unit ρ scaled by info.scale.Msol_pc3
getvar(gas, :rho_msun_pc3, :standard)    # call-time unit override → code units
```

### Other data types

By default fields are registered for hydro. Register for other kinds (or several at once)
with `datatypes`:

```julia
add_field(:speed, (o, d) -> sqrt.(d[:vx].^2 .+ d[:vy].^2 .+ d[:vz].^2);
          depends_on = [:vx, :vy, :vz], datatypes = [:hydro, :particle])
```

Valid kinds: `:hydro`, `:gravity`, `:rt`, `:particle`, `:clump`.

## Managing registered fields

```julia
list_fields(:hydro)                 # names you added for hydro (custom only)
list_fields(:hydro; builtin=true)   # built-in derived fields ∪ your custom ones, sorted
field_info(:vmag2)                  # (; compute, depends_on, unit, description)
delete_field(:vmag2)                # remove it (delete_field(name; datatypes=:all) by default)
```

`list_fields(kind; builtin=true)` is the quickest way to discover what you can ask `getvar` for on a
given data type, it returns the dependency-registry built-ins together with any fields you registered.
It covers most but not every built-in quantity (a few specialised fields are computed directly in
`getvar`); for the complete human-readable catalogue call `getvar()` with no arguments.

The **default** (`builtin=false`) lists only the fields *you* registered, so it starts empty and grows
as you `add_field` (and shrinks again on `delete_field`):

```@example listdefault
using Mera          # hide
list_fields(:hydro)                 # builtin=false (default): custom fields only — none yet
```

```@example listdefault
add_field(:speed2, (o, d) -> d[:vx].^2 .+ d[:vy].^2 .+ d[:vz].^2; depends_on=[:vx, :vy, :vz])
list_fields(:hydro)                 # the field you just added now appears
```

```@example listdefault
delete_field(:speed2)
list_fields(:hydro)                 # removed again → back to empty
```

With `builtin=true` the same call instead returns the full catalogue. The lists below are generated
live from the registry at doc-build time, so they always match the installed version. **Hydro:**

```@example fields
using Mera          # hide
list_fields(:hydro; builtin=true)
```

**Gravity, RT, particle, clump** (same call, different `kind`):

```@example fields
list_fields(:gravity;  builtin=true)
```

```@example fields
list_fields(:particle; builtin=true)
```

```@example fields
(rt = list_fields(:rt; builtin=true), clump = list_fields(:clump; builtin=true))
```

!!! note "Registry scope"
    Registered fields live for the current Julia session (they are not persisted to disk).
    Put your `add_field` calls in a startup script or at the top of your analysis to make them
    available every run.

Registered fields also work as quantities in [First-Look Reports](report.md) cards, the report reads
only the dependencies your field declares.

## Custom units

A field's `unit` can be an existing `info.scale` field, `:standard`, a plain **number** (a literal
code→display factor), or a **custom unit** you register with [`add_unit`](@ref). Registered units work
everywhere a unit is accepted, including `getvar(obj, var, unit)` for built-in quantities:

```julia
add_unit(:Msun_per_century, 1e-2)               # 1 code-unit value × 1e-2
add_field(:mdot, (o,d) -> d[:rho]; depends_on=[:rho], unit=:Msun_per_century)
getvar(gas, :mass, :Msun_per_century)           # also applies to built-in fields
list_units();  delete_unit(:Msun_per_century)
```

## Inspecting dependencies

```julia
field_dependencies(:hydro, :ekin)   # (; direct=[:mass,:v], raw=[:rho,:vx,:vy,:vz])
field_tree(:hydro, :mach)           # prints the dependency tree down to raw leaves
```
```
mach
├─ v
│  ├─ vx  (raw)
│  ├─ vy  (raw)
│  └─ vz  (raw)
└─ cs
   ├─ p  (raw)
   └─ rho  (raw)
```

## See also

Registered fields are used throughout Mera: [`getvar`](@ref) computes them, [`projection`](@ref) and
[`profile`](@ref) read only the dependencies they need (via [`getvar_requirements`](@ref)), and the
[First Look](report.md) (`quicklook` / `report`) verbs benefit from the same needs-based
reading. See also [Star-Formation Rate](sfr.md) and [Clump Finding](clumpfind.md) for fields used in
analysis.

## API

```@docs
add_field
delete_field
list_fields
field_info
field_dependencies
field_tree
add_unit
delete_unit
list_units
getvar_requirements
```


<!-- ===== bundled_arguments.md ===== -->

# Bundling Arguments (`myargs`)

Many Mera functions share the same arguments: a spatial region, a center, a resolution, the
verbose/progress switches. Repeating them on every `gethydro`, `getparticles`, `projection`,
`subregion`, … call is verbose and error-prone. [`ArgumentsType`](@ref) lets you fill them in
**once** and pass the whole bundle as the single keyword `myargs=…`.

## The idea

```julia
using Mera
info = getinfo(300, "/data/Mera-Tests/mw_L10", verbose=false)

# 1. make an (empty) argument bundle
myargs = ArgumentsType()

# 2. fill only the fields you need
myargs.pxsize     = [100., :pc]
myargs.xrange     = [-10., 10.]
myargs.yrange     = [-10., 10.]
myargs.zrange     = [-2., 2.]
myargs.center     = [:boxcenter]
myargs.range_unit = :kpc

# 3. reuse it everywhere — no repetition
gas  = gethydro(info,  myargs=myargs)
part = getparticles(info, myargs=myargs)
p    = projection(gas, :sd, :Msun_pc2, myargs=myargs)
```

`ArgumentsType` also takes the same fields as keywords, which is shorter when you know them
up front:

```julia
myargs = ArgumentsType(pxsize=[100., :pc], xrange=[-10., 10.], yrange=[-10., 10.],
                       zrange=[-2., 2.], center=[:boxcenter], range_unit=:kpc)
```

Every field left `missing` is ignored, so a bundle only overrides what you set. A value you
pass **explicitly** still wins over the bundle, so you can share a base bundle and tweak one
call:

```julia
projection(gas, :sd, :Msun_pc2, myargs=myargs, pxsize=[50., :pc])   # 50 pc, not the bundle's 100
```

Override with the *same* keyword the bundle sets. Passing a different one that
means the same thing does not work: the bundle above sets `pxsize`, and
`pxsize` takes precedence over `res`, so adding `res=512` to that call would be
ignored rather than overriding anything.

!!! note "One edge case"
    Mera decides that you passed a value explicitly by seeing that it differs
    from the function's own default. So passing a value that *equals* the
    default, `verbose=true` where `true` is already the default, does not
    override a bundle that sets it to `false`. Leave such a field out of the
    bundle if you want to vary it per call.

See the current contents of a bundle with [`viewfields`](@ref):

```julia
viewfields(myargs)
```

## Deriving a variant: `withargs`

A bundle is mutable, so changing a field changes it for every later call. When you want a
variant, [`withargs`](@ref) returns a **copy** with some fields replaced and leaves the
original alone:

```julia
base   = ArgumentsType(lmax=10, xrange=[-10., 10.], center=[:boxcenter], range_unit=:kpc)

coarse = withargs(base; lmax=7)                            # same region, fewer levels
zoom   = withargs(base; xrange=[-2., 2.], yrange=[-2., 2.])  # same levels, smaller region

gas    = gethydro(info, myargs=base)
gas_c  = gethydro(info, myargs=coarse)
```

`base` is untouched in both cases. The copy is deep, so editing `zoom.xrange` in place cannot
reach back into `base`.

Without it you would write `deepcopy` and then an assignment, and a plain assignment
(`variant = base`) is the trap: it gives you the *same* bundle under a second name, and the
next field you set changes both.

```julia
variant = base            # NOT a copy: variant and base are one object
variant = withargs(base)  # a copy, safe to change
```

## What you can bundle

`ArgumentsType` collects the arguments shared across the loading, region, and projection
functions:

| group | fields |
|-------|--------|
| region | `xrange`, `yrange`, `zrange`, `center`, `range_unit`, `radius`, `height` |
| resolution / level | `pxsize`, `res`, `lmax` |
| projection view | `direction`, `los`, `up`, `theta`, `phi`, `inclination`, `azimuth`, `position_angle`, `axis`, `angle_unit` |
| slice / plane | `plane`, `plane_ranges`, `thickness`, `position`, `data_center`, `data_center_unit` |
| binning | `binning`, `nmax` |
| output | `verbose`, `show_progress`, `verbose_threads` |

!!! note
    Any function that accepts these arguments accepts the `myargs` bundle: `getinfo`,
    `gethydro`/`getparticles`/`getgravity`/`getclumps`/`getrt`, `subregion`/`shellregion`,
    `projection`, [`loadall`](@ref), and the data converters. `getsinks` is the exception: a
    sink catalogue has no spatial selection to apply, so it takes no bundle.

## A silent, reusable bundle

Because the bundle includes `verbose` and `show_progress`: you can make a "quiet" preset and
apply it to a batch of calls:

```julia
quiet = ArgumentsType()
quiet.verbose       = false
quiet.show_progress = false

gas  = gethydro(info, myargs=quiet)
part = getparticles(info, myargs=quiet)
```

For silencing **all** Mera calls at once (without threading a bundle through each): use the
global switch instead: see [Verbose & progress switches](verbose_progress_switches.md).

## Other ways to bundle: and when `myargs` is the right one

Julia itself has a first-class way to bundle keyword arguments: a `NamedTuple` **splatted**
with `;`. It works directly with Mera functions, no special type needed:

```julia
opts = (; xrange=[-10.,10.], yrange=[-10.,10.], center=[:boxcenter], range_unit=:kpc)

gas = gethydro(info; opts...)                 # splat the bundle as keywords
p   = projection(gas, :sd; opts...)

gethydro(info; opts..., lmax=6)               # an explicit keyword overrides the bundle
gethydro(info; merge(opts, (; lmax=6))...)    # …or merge first, then splat
```

This is the idiomatic choice for a bundle of options shared by **one** function, or by
functions that all accept the **same** keywords.

There is one important difference. A splatted `NamedTuple` passes *every* key as a keyword,
so a key the target function does **not** accept is an error:

```julia
opts2 = (; xrange=[-10.,10.], los=[0.,0.,1.])   # los is a projection-only argument
gethydro(info; opts2...)                         # ERROR: gethydro has no `los` keyword
```

[`ArgumentsType`](@ref) (`myargs`) is built exactly for this case: it is a **tolerant,
heterogeneous** bundle. Each function reads only the fields it knows and ignores the rest, so
**one** bundle can carry arguments for several functions with *different* signatures:

```julia
ma = ArgumentsType()
ma.xrange = [-10.,10.]; ma.center = [:boxcenter]; ma.range_unit = :kpc
ma.los = [0.,0.,1.]                  # only projection uses this

gethydro(info, myargs=ma)            # ignores `los`, uses the region
projection(gas, :sd, myargs=ma)      # uses `los` and the region
```

Rule of thumb:

| you want | use |
|----------|-----|
| share options across calls of the **same** function (or same keywords) | a `NamedTuple` + `; opts...` (native Julia) |
| override a shared bundle for one call | `; opts..., key=val` or `merge(opts, (; key=val))...` |
| **one** bundle spanning functions with **different** signatures | `myargs=ArgumentsType()` (tolerant) |
| a preconfigured shorthand function | a closure, `myhydro(info; kw...) = gethydro(info; opts..., kw...)` |

You can also combine them: pass a `myargs` bundle *and* splat a `NamedTuple` of extra
keywords in the same call.

## See also

- [Verbose & progress switches](verbose_progress_switches.md): global master switch for messages and progress bars.
- [`gethydro`](@ref), [`projection`](@ref), [`subregion`](@ref): the functions that accept `myargs`.
- [`withargs`](@ref): derive a variant of a bundle without touching the original.
- [Pipelines](pipelines.md): bundles combined with `loadall` and the projection macros.
- [Gallery](gallery.md): complete workflows that use a bundle across a whole analysis.
